title: 160-bay NVMe SSD 4U Server Shown at FMS 2026 Supermicro ASG-4116S-NU160R
gist: At FMS 2026 Supermicro showed the ASG-4116S-NU160R, a single-socket AMD EPYC 9005 4U server with 160 U.2 NVMe bays that reaches roughly 19-20PB when filled with 122TB-class SSDs such as Solidigm's D5-P5336, at an estimated $8-10M per box. The architecture substitutes PCIe switches for the SAS expanders of traditional top-loading storage, trading peak per-drive throughput for lower per-drive power, and lands at only 130-137W per petabyte at the outlet through redundant 2.6kW supplies — less than the power the 500 hard drives needed for equivalent capacity would draw.

insights.claim: Supermicro's ASG-4116S-NU160R packs 160 U.2 NVMe drive bays into 4U, and when populated with 122-128TB-class SSDs it reaches roughly 19-20PB of raw capacity in a single chassis.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: 20PB per 4U resets the ceiling on flash density per rack unit and is the concrete number to benchmark competing all-flash array vendors and HDD-based capacity tiers against.
insights.quote: The Supermicro ASG-4116S-NU160R is a single-socket AMD EPYC server that sports 160x U.2 NVMe drive bays. Taking only 4U of space
insights.locator: At FMS 2026, we saw a really neat system

insights.claim: The Solidigm D5-P5336 at 122.88TB is cited as the class of drive that makes ~20PB in a single 4U chassis achievable today, meaning the capacity record depends on QLC high-capacity SSD supply.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Systems like this convert directly into unit demand for 100TB+ SSDs; Solidigm and peers shipping that class of drive capture disproportionate value per chassis sold.
insights.quote: combined with even “just” 122-128TB class NVMe SSDs, like the Solidigm D5-P5336 122.88TB NVMe SSD we reviewed, this is roughly 20PB of storage in a single system.
insights.locator: At FMS 2026, we saw a really neat system

insights.claim: The reviewer estimates a fully populated ASG-4116S-NU160R with 122TB-class SSDs is an $8-10M machine, putting the implied cost of high-capacity flash at roughly $400-500K per petabyte in this configuration.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: An eight-figure single-chassis price tag shows the SSD bill of materials, not the server, is the deal value — server OEM revenue per rack is small relative to the NAND content it pulls through.
insights.quote: this is likely an $8-10M machine with 122TB-class SSDs putting it into the 19-20PB in 4U range
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: The ASG-4116S-NU160R was the densest storage platform on the FMS 2026 show floor according to the reviewer's survey of the event.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Establishes a public competitive benchmark and a date stamp; any rival announcing higher 4U density after August 2026 is measurably leapfrogging Supermicro.
insights.quote: At FMS, this was the densest storage platform we could find.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: The drive shelf holds rows of 10 drives on either side of a center column, and slide-out trays split the system with SSDs on top and CPU, memory and networking below.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Serviceable slide-out trays are the mechanical prerequisite for top-loading flash at this density; chassis and rail-kit mechanics become a differentiator as bay counts rise.
insights.quote: Slide-out trays are important in top-loading storage systems because they allow servicing without pulling the entire system out of the rack.
insights.locator: Supermicro ASG-4116S-NU160R Overview

insights.claim: Wiring 160 NVMe devices at four lanes each would require 640 PCIe lanes before counting NICs, far beyond any single CPU's lane budget, so Supermicro places PCIe switches in the chassis center column to fan out connectivity.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Every step up in NVMe bay count multiplies PCIe switch content per chassis — a direct demand driver for PCIe switch silicon vendors as flash density scales.
insights.quote: As you might imagine, 160x NVMe devices all running with four lanes would require 640 PCIe lanes, and that is without NICs to move data on and off of the system.
insights.locator: In the center section, there are PCIe switches

insights.claim: The design is architecturally a top-loading SAS storage server with PCIe switches substituted for SAS expanders, showing the SAS-era chassis playbook migrating wholesale to NVMe.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for the transition: dense-storage chassis topology stays constant while the fan-out silicon shifts from SAS to PCIe, which is bearish for SAS expander vendors and bullish for PCIe switch suppliers.
insights.quote: Supermicro’s solution is to use a setup similar to what we would expect from a top-loading SAS storage server, but instead of SAS expanders, it is using PCIe switches.
insights.locator: Supermicro Asg 4116S Nu160R 2.5 Pcie 4.0 Nvme Drive Bay 3

insights.claim: Oversubscribing drives behind PCIe switches means individual SSDs will not hit their maximum sequential throughput, an explicit performance trade the design accepts in exchange for density.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: This is a capacity-tier machine, not a performance-tier one; buyers displacing HDD nearline capacity are the target market, not those chasing peak IOPS per drive.
insights.quote: the PCIe switch architecture means that each drive will not achieve its maximum sequential throughput
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: Limiting PCIe lanes per drive lets each SSD run at lower power, so the switch-based oversubscription that costs throughput simultaneously buys back the thermal and power budget needed to fit 160 drives in 4U.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: A non-obvious second-order effect: lane throttling is a power lever, meaning extreme-density flash designs are viable inside standard rack power envelopes without exotic cooling.
insights.quote: By limiting the lanes to each drive, the drives can run at lower power.
insights.locator: Final Words

themes.theme: Watts per petabyte versus hard drives

insights.claim: The entire 160-drive system including SSDs, NICs and CPU runs off redundant 2.6kW power supplies, working out to roughly 130-137W per petabyte of storage measured at the outlet.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: 130-137W/PB is a hard benchmark for datacenter capacity planning; in power-constrained AI facilities, storage watts freed up are directly convertible into accelerator watts.
insights.quote: Call that only 130-137W per PB of storage all-in at the outlet, which seems quite amazing.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: The full 4U flash system's power envelope sits below what the roughly 500 hard drives needed for equivalent capacity would consume on their own, before counting the servers and enclosures to host them.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: The long-standing assumption that HDDs win on capacity-tier TCO breaks once power is priced properly; watch for capacity-tier flash displacing nearline HDD in power-constrained sites, a structural risk to HDD makers.
insights.quote: That power envelope is below just the power required to drive the 500 hard drives you would need for a similar capacity.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: Matching the 160-bay chassis with conventional 24-bay 2U servers would take about seven of them for 168 bays, so the dense design eliminates roughly six CPUs and 72 DIMMs' worth of infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: With DRAM and CPU prices elevated, consolidation savings — not rack space — are the real purchase justification; this reduces incremental server-CPU and DIMM demand per petabyte deployed.
insights.quote: If you had 24-bay 2U servers, you would need 7 or so of them (168 bays total) to have a similar capacity. So this design saves you roughly 6 CPUs and 72 DIMMs over using standard 2U servers.
insights.locator: One of the other interesting bits is that the system uses a single AMD EPYC 9005 CPU

insights.claim: The system drives all 160 NVMe bays from a single AMD EPYC 9005 CPU rated up to 360W, showing one modern server CPU can anchor 20PB of flash.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Single-socket EPYC winning the dense-storage head node is a share datapoint for AMD, but the CPU-per-petabyte ratio collapsing is a headwind to server CPU unit volumes in storage tiers.
insights.quote: the system uses a single AMD EPYC 9005 CPU up to 360W
insights.locator: One of the other interesting bits

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that eliminating redundant CPUs and DIMMs is the actual purpose of ultra-dense storage servers, not merely saving rack units.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Reframes the dense-storage category as a component-cost arbitrage play, which means its adoption tracks DRAM and CPU pricing rather than datacenter floor-space scarcity.
insights.quote: Perhaps that is really the point of all of these servers.
insights.locator: One of the other interesting bits

insights.claim: Beyond the 160 U.2 bays the chassis adds four E1.S NVMe bays on the front panel alongside the IPMI port, dual USB and two 10Gbase-T ports built on the Broadcom BCM57416.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: E1.S appearing as boot/cache media even in a U.2-based capacity chassis marks EDSFF's beachhead; Broadcom's controller in the management/base networking slot is quiet but recurring silicon content.
insights.quote: There are four E1.S NVMe SSD bays on the front panel next to the IPMI port, dual USB ports, and then two 10Gbase-T ports (Broadcom BCM57416).
insights.locator: When we say this is a 160-SSD design, that is technically selling it short

insights.claim: The CPU tray exposes three available PCIe Gen5 x16 slots explicitly sized for 400GbE NICs and DPUs, so front-end network bandwidth rather than drive count governs how fast data moves off the box.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Each such chassis pulls through up to three 400GbE-class adapters, tying dense-flash deployments directly to high-speed NIC and DPU vendors' unit demand.
insights.quote: There are three available PCIe Gen5 x16 slots for your 400GbE NICs and DPUs in this system.
insights.locator: The CPU tray pulls out as well

insights.claim: Placing the four E1.S bays and full-height expansion slots between the VGA and USB ports creates a practical serviceability problem when a technician hooks a KVM cart to the machine in the cold aisle.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Front-panel congestion at extreme density raises operational friction; serviceability is emerging as a real differentiator once bay counts pass 100 per chassis.
insights.quote: it must be interesting when you have a KVM cart in the cold aisle and hook up to one of these
insights.locator: When we say this is a 160-SSD design

themes.theme: SSD-embedded DRAM as the next cost target

insights.claim: A fully populated 160-drive chassis contains roughly 5TB of DRAM embedded inside the SSDs themselves, an amount of memory buried in drive controllers that rivals a large server's main memory.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Quantifies a hidden DRAM sink inside high-capacity SSDs — meaningful incremental DRAM demand per petabyte deployed, and an obvious cost-reduction target if DRAM prices stay elevated.
insights.quote: It also would house something like 5TB of memory just in the NVMe SSDs.
insights.locator: Final Words

insights.claim: The article points to a Sandisk prototype drive that, deployed in an E3.S version of this kind of platform, is framed as removing about $300K of DRAM from a single storage server while saving over 10kW for AI factories.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: If DRAM-less or reduced-DRAM SSD architectures reach volume, they cut both server BOM and power in AI buildouts — a potential demand headwind for DRAM makers and a differentiation lever for Sandisk.
insights.quote:
Sandisk’s Plan to Remove $300K of DRAM from a Single Storage Server by Patrick Kennedy
…and save over 10kW for AI factories using that type of server.
insights.locator: Final Words, closing link

insights.claim: Elevated memory prices are given as the explicit reason dense-flash platforms are being reconsidered around DRAM-reduced SSD designs, tying storage architecture choices to the DRAM cost cycle.
insights.speaker: Eric Smith
insights.so_what: Watch DRAM spot pricing as a leading indicator for adoption of DRAM-less SSD controller architectures in capacity-tier storage.
insights.quote: Given memory prices, we actually used this server as an example of how Sandisk’s innovative prototype drive in a platform like this server (with E3.S SSDs instead) could deliver massive DRAM savings in the future.
insights.locator: Final Words
